title: I Took the Maple-Sap Evaporator Booking to the Chair Who Left My Draw

parts.text: I opened the sugarhouse at 5:04 a.m. and chair Bram was already drawing from my numbered pan. The slate said: ONE PAN. FOUR HOURS. DRAW STAYS WITH THE BOOKING. I was forty-nine, sugarhouse volunteer, holding a hydrometer that listed our run. Bram shrugged. "Chairs are the steam." I photographed the slate, the booking, and his dipper in my syrup. Then I asked for the evaporator log. At 5:12 the house pinged why Bram's name was on my draw. I kept my voice steam-quiet and let the timestamp talk. A slate is only a slate until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The house can see Bram's dipper in my syrup during our booking.

social.video_title: He drew from my numbered pan on my run — Part 1/2
social.description: Sugarhouse, a chair in my syrup, a four-hour slate he posted. I logged the dipper. Would you have asked for the evaporator log?

parts.text: Bram called it a taste until the house asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the slate, and the dipper still. The draw went back to my hydrometer. Bram ran his own four hours and told the next chair atmosphere was always about grade. Grade is a word chairs use when a booking exists. Pan policy now has a second line: CHAIRS ARE NOT THE STEAM. I keep our run on a labeled jug. Bram brown-bags his jokes. The house finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.description: Evaporator log, numbered pan, and a second line on the slate. Was a taste ever my draw?
